Bay Raises $50 Million to Stop AI Agents From Making Dangerous Decisions Inside Companies
Epil Bodra
| November 11 | Business Stories , Funding Feed
Share
Cybersecurity startup Bay has emerged from stealth with $50 million in funding , just nine months after its founding, as businesses face growing security risks from autonomous AI agents operating across corporate systems.
The company, founded in early 2026 by former Israeli intelligence and cybersecurity professionals, has developed technology designed to detect and block potentially harmful actions by AI agents, including those operating with legitimate access permissions.
The funding includes a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures , with participation from Micron Ventures, Microsoft’s venture capital arm M12, and Wiz CEO Assaf Rappaport. Bay also disclosed an earlier $13 million seed round backed by YL Ventures and Striker.
Cisco Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel and former Zscaler Chief Strategy Officer Manoj Apte are among the company’s private investors.
Bay was established by CEO Yuval Zacharia, Chief Product Officer Aner Morag , and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich.
The founders identified a critical security problem after one of their own AI coding agents attempted to expose a cloud environment to the public internet while completing a test.
The agent had not been compromised, nor was it acting under instructions from an attacker. Instead, it was using authorized permissions to accomplish its assigned task, potentially creating a serious security vulnerability in the process.
That experience became the foundation for Bay’s approach to AI security, which focuses on preventing dangerous actions even when an agent is functioning as intended.
Unlike traditional security systems that primarily focus on unauthorized access or malicious activity, Bay examines what an AI agent is attempting to accomplish and whether its actions could violate an organization’s security policies.
Its platform discovers AI agents operating across corporate environments and analyzes their activities within the context of an entire session, including their assigned objectives and previous actions.
Based on that information, the system can approve an action, block it, or refer it for human authorization. Bay says these decisions occur locally within milliseconds, allowing permitted operations to continue without disrupting workflows.
The technology supports AI assistants, coding agents, custom-built agents, and the tools they use across employee devices, cloud infrastructure, and software-as-a-service applications.
Bay also claims its platform can be deployed in under five minutes using existing corporate security infrastructure, without installing additional persistent endpoint agents or network proxies.
The company says its technology is already being used by dozens of enterprise customers across finance, insurance, manufacturing, media, and technology.
Wix, ClickUp, Micron, and Peloton are among its named customers. Micron is also participating in the company’s latest funding round through Micron Ventures.
Zacharia told Calcalist that Bay’s rapid fundraising was supported by early customer demand and revenue growth. She said the company generated millions in revenue during its first quarter of sales, although an exact figure was not disclosed.

Bay Emerges From Stealth With $50M After Fortune 100 Companies Used Its Platform to Triple Autonomous AI Agent Use
By James Dargan · 13 November 2026 · 5 min read
Insider Brief
Bay, an AI security platform for agentic enterprises, has emerged from stealth with $50 million in total funding, including a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures and a $13 million seed led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners.
The Tel Aviv-based company evaluates each AI agent action in the context of the full session and decides in milliseconds whether it can proceed, deploying across devices, cloud and SaaS in under five minutes without extra endpoint agents or network proxies.
Founded less than a year ago by Yuval Zacharia, Aner Morag and Boris Danilovich, Bay already counts Micron, Peloton, ClickUp and Wix among its customers and will use the funding to expand its teams in the US and Europe.
PRESS RELEASE —  Bay , the AI security platform building the trust layer for agentic enterprises, has emerged from stealth less than a year after its founding with dozens of enterprise customers, including Micron, Peloton, ClickUp and Wix. Bay addresses a primary barrier to AI adoption by allowing autonomous agents to perform business-critical work safely while enterprises retain control and accountability at scale.
Bay has raised $50 million in total funding. The financing includes a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures and a previously undisclosed $13 million seed led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners. Micron Ventures, M12, Microsoft’s Venture Fund and Assaf Rappaport, CEO of Wiz, also participated in the Series A.
“AI is fundamentally changing how enterprises operate, and the ability to deploy autonomous agents safely will become a critical competitive advantage,” said Andrew Byrnes, Director of Venture Capital, Micron. “We’ve seen firsthand how Bay’s technology can help accelerate AI adoption while maintaining the control and accountability required in a large enterprise. We believe that this trust layer will become essential infrastructure for the agentic era.”
Bay grew out of the same problem it now solves for customers. Its founders watched one of their coding agents try to expose a cloud environment to the internet to complete a test. The agent had not been compromised. It used legitimate permissions to pursue a legitimate goal in a dangerous way.
Bay brings AI governance and enforcement across employee devices, cloud infrastructure, and SaaS applications in under 5 minutes, without an additional persistent endpoint agent, kernel driver, or network proxy. It secures the full range of AI that enterprises are deploying through a single platform that covers multiple use cases under one set of policies. Bay combines AI discovery and posture management, session-level observability, and real-time enforcement, and connects to existing security workflows for automated remediation.
“In Bay, we saw a company we felt had a differentiated technical approach that was already winning enterprise customers at an early stage,” said Dharmesh Thakker, General Partner at Battery Ventures. “That combination gave us conviction to lead the round. We believe Bay can become a core control layer for companies putting AI agents to work at scale.”

Bay raises $50 million for enterprise AI agent security
Tel Aviv-based Bay has secured $50 million in funding to launch its enterprise AI agent security platform. The platform discovers AI agents and enforces policies at runtime, preventing unintended actions.
TechGig
Published On Nov 13, 2026 at 06:00 AM IST
Share Icon
Copy Link Share on Whatsapp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook
Bookmark
Comment
Highlights
Bay secured $50 million in funding for its enterprise AI agent security platform.
The platform discovers AI agents and enforces policies at runtime.
It prevents unintended actions from prompt injection or agent purpose drift.
Deployment is agentless and takes under five minutes across an entire fleet.
Tel Aviv-based Bay has emerged from stealth with $50 million in funding, comprising a $37 million Series A round led by Battery Ventures and a $13 million seed funding round led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners.
Bay was founded in February 2026 by Yuval Zacharia, Boris Danilovich, and Aner Morag, all alumni of the Israeli Military Intelligence (IDF Unit 8200). The company’s platform provides a single control plane that discovers, understands, and controls AI agents wherever they run within an enterprise.
Upon installation, Bay automatically inventories AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, skills, extensions, and local models in use. It also maps their connections, including potentially risky tool combinations.
The platform’s Enforcer component evaluates every proposed agent action in milliseconds within the context of the full session. It decides whether to allow, refer to the user, redirect based on policy, or deny the action.
Bay’s embedded AI system, Lighthouse, automatically builds and maintains policies based on the organisation’s activity history. This system protects against dangerous agent activity, whether caused by malicious prompt injection or organic agent purpose drift.
Bay’s CEO and co-founder Yuval Zacharia told SecurityWeek that effortless deployment, immediate time to value, and clear operationalisation were non-negotiable design principles. The company built a flexible, agentless architecture for deployment across an entire fleet in under five minutes.
Its patented technology retrospectively analyses 30 days of historical logs. This allows customers to see Bay’s potential value and complete a proof of value in less than 14 days. The funding will support product development, engineering team expansion, and go-to-market plans in the US and Europe.

Index Industries Raises $50 Million in Funding to Reinvent How the World Invests in Real Estate
News provided by
Index Industries
Nov 10, 2026, 12:00 ET
Share this article
Share this article
Index Industries is co-founded by Josh Rosenthal, formerly the President of Polychain Capital, joining as CEO, and Brian Hardecker, CEO of Longmark and formerly of Blackstone, joining as Chairman.
The round is backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners, Galaxy Ventures, Polychain Capital, Wintermute Ventures and more.
Index Industries will launch the USHP Index, a proprietary benchmark for U.S. home prices, made investable through USHP, a liquid index product, issued by USHP Limited.
NEW YORK , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Index Industries emerges from stealth with a $50 million seed round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from Polychain Capital, Galaxy Ventures, Wintermute Ventures, and other institutional investors. The company is building the technology and infrastructure to transform U.S. housing into a broadly investable asset class. Its platform combines a daily-reporting index with tokenization technology and real estate and capital markets services to power third-party housing-linked investment products. USHP , based on Index Industries' U.S. Home Price Index and issued by USHP Limited (BVI), will be the first investment product built on the platform.
U.S. housing is a $55 trillion market, making it one of the largest asset classes in the U.S. Yet despite its scale, broad-based investment exposure to U.S. home prices has remained difficult to access through traditional financial products. Index Industries was founded to close that gap.
Index Industries' first offering will be the U.S. Home Price Index (USHP Index), a proprietary benchmark for U.S. home prices. Calculated daily, it integrates data from the major housing indices into a single national measure, providing a continuous and comprehensive read on home prices. The index is intended to support housing-market research, reporting, and portfolio monitoring and housing-related financial products.
Index Industries is co-founded by Josh Rosenthal, who joins as CEO following his role as President and General Partner of Polychain Capital, and Brian Hardecker, a former Principal at Blackstone and the Founder and CEO of Longmark, a leading residential real estate platform formed in 2021 that has $2 billion in assets under management. Index Industries combines two worlds of expertise to bring breakthrough tokenization technology to new real estate assets.
"Indexing is one of the most important and least celebrated innovations in modern finance. It reduces the expertise and cost barriers to investing in an entire market, which is what U.S. housing needs," said Josh Rosenthal, co-founder & CEO of Index Industries. "I've spent my career looking for industry-shaping financial technology, and Index Industries is exactly that. It has the potential to change how the world sees housing: not just as a roof over your head or something that is out of reach, but as an investable asset class."
"U.S. housing is a massive market. It accounts for roughly a quarter of the aggregate value of the U.S. economy, yet it draws far less attention because there haven't been accessible ways to take a position in it," said Brian Hardecker, co-founder and chairman of Index Industries and CEO of Longmark Group. Optics11: €50 Million Funding To Expand Underwater Defense And Energy Grid Sensing Technology
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 1:07 AM
Optics11: €50 Million Funding To Expand Underwater Defense And Energy Grid Sensing Technology
Optics11, an Amsterdam-based deep technology company developing fiber-optic sensing systems for maritime security and energy infrastructure, has secured €50 million in follow-on equity financing. The investment brings the company’s total capital raised over the past 15 months to more than €100 million and will support manufacturing expansion, international growth, and increased deployment of its sensing technologies.
The latest financing was backed by existing institutional investors FORWARD.one, Value Creation Capital, SET Ventures, and JOIN Capital, with all four participating in the new round.
The investment comes as governments, defense organizations, and infrastructure operators seek additional capabilities to protect underwater assets and strengthen electricity networks.
Optics11 develops fiber-optic sensing systems designed to detect underwater activity, identify potential security threats, and monitor conditions within critical energy infrastructure.
The company’s technology originated from research at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, where its underlying photonics and acoustics capabilities were developed before Optics11 was founded in 2011.
Its sensing approach uses light to detect small acoustic signals rather than relying on powered electronics at the measurement location.
This design enables highly sensitive monitoring while remaining passive and resistant to electromagnetic interference.
The technology has applications across maritime surveillance, subsea infrastructure protection, and electrical grid monitoring.
Expanding Maritime Defense Capabilities
Optics11 is developing products intended to strengthen underwater surveillance and anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
Its OptiBarrier system provides persistent seabed sensing designed to detect and classify underwater targets at distances of up to 100 kilometers from the shoreline.
The system is intended to provide ongoing monitoring of sensitive maritime areas and infrastructure.
The company’s OptiArray platform extends its fiber-optic sensing capabilities into a mobile towed array that can be deployed from vessels.
OptiArray supports underwater intelligence gathering, maritime surveillance, and anti-submarine warfare operations.
Earlier in 2026, the Dutch Ministry of Defence selected Optics11’s containerized OptiArray technology for the ASWINABO program, also known as Anti-Submarine Warfare In A Box.
The program aims to provide advanced underwater sensing capabilities through a wider range of maritime platforms.
These include crewed and uncrewed surface vessels, as well as certain civilian ships.
The initiative is intended to improve the Royal Netherlands Navy’s readiness and operational flexibility.
Optics11 considers the selection an important validation of its technology and a potential foundation for additional defense deployments.
The company sees increased interest in maritime sensing systems as European governments reassess their ability to monitor underwater activity and protect critical infrastructure.
Strengthening Electricity Grid Monitoring
Optics11 also applies its sensing technology to electrical infrastructure through its OptiFinder platform.

articles.text:
Courier Health: Three Executives Appointed To Support Growth
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 12:38 PM
Courier Health: Three Executives Appointed To Support Growth
Courier Health has appointed three executives to oversee its commercial, people, and customer success organizations following its $50 million Series B funding round.
Eben Scanlon joined the patient experience technology company as chief commercial officer. Mike Lamm was named chief people officer, while Phil Mishkin became senior vice president of customer success.
Scanlon will lead Courier Health’s sales and marketing teams. He previously helped clinical trial technology company Reify Health grow from an early-stage business to hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. His prior experience also includes positions at Medidata, VMware, and McKinsey & Company.
Lamm will oversee recruiting, talent development, and employee retention. He helped Squarespace prepare for and complete its public listing, supported monday.com’s expansion across the Americas, and most recently served as chief people officer at behavioral healthcare technology company RethinkFirst.
Mishkin will lead Courier Health’s post-sale organization, encompassing customer success, implementation, customer engineering, and value engineering. During eight years at Komodo Health, he built its customer success operation as the company’s customer base expanded by more than 100 times.
The appointments follow a year of increased adoption for Courier Health’s AI-native patient experience platform. The company recently introduced AI Intake and previewed AI Appeal, agents designed to automate work associated with patient enrollment and prior authorization denial appeals.
Courier Health develops software for biopharmaceutical companies managing patient access, treatment initiation, and adherence. Customers using its platform have reported double-digit improvements in patient starts, time to treatment, and continued therapy use.
The company expects its expanded leadership team to support demand from life sciences organizations seeking to modernize patient services.
KEY QUOTES
“Biopharma is rethinking how it supports patients, and the industry is increasingly turning to Courier Health to lead that shift. To meet the demand ahead, we’re bringing in leaders who have done this before.”
Danny Sigurdson, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Courier Health

articles.title: Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
articles.snippet:
Arcturus Therapeutics has expanded its collaboration with Meiji Seika Pharma through a $50 million equity investment, an additional technology license and a proposed pandemic preparedness partnership in Japan.
The post Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
articles.text:
Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 4:20 PM
Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
Arcturus Therapeutics has expanded its collaboration with Meiji Seika Pharma through a $50 million equity investment, an additional technology license and a proposed pandemic preparedness partnership in Japan.
Meiji will purchase unregistered Arcturus securities at $20.27 per share, an 80% premium under the announced transaction terms. Its investment will represent approximately 7.9% of outstanding shares following the transaction.
The companies also signed an exclusive license covering the application of Arcturus’s ARCT-154 technology in an undisclosed therapeutic area.
Separately, a memorandum of understanding establishes principal terms for a potential collaboration and license agreement involving pandemic preparedness and response in Japan. That arrangement remains subject to a definitive agreement.
Arcturus intends to use the investment to support its cystic fibrosis program and accelerate ARCT-2601, an investigational treatment for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.
ARCT-2601 is the first mRNA therapeutic intended to use the company’s LUNAR 2.0 delivery platform. Its development is expected to contribute to clinical evaluation of that next-generation technology.
President and CEO Joseph Payne said the expanded relationship reflects Meiji’s confidence in the company’s capabilities and platform.
Founded in 2013 and based in San Diego, Arcturus develops mRNA medicines focused on liver and respiratory diseases.
Its technologies include lipid-mediated delivery and self-amplifying RNA. The company also developed KOSTAIVE, a self-amplifying mRNA COVID vaccine.
Other collaborations include work with Thermo Fisher Scientific, BARDA and Japanese manufacturing joint venture ARCALIS.
Meiji’s investment adds capital while extending an existing strategic relationship across development, licensing and potential public-health applications.
The company’s pipeline programs remain subject to clinical development, regulatory review and other requirements before potential commercialization.
KEY QUOTES
“We are pleased to expand our relationship with Meiji as we advance innovative mRNA medicines and seek to deliver value to patients. The investment, together with the license agreement and the pandemic preparedness MOU, reflects Meiji’s confidence in our development capabilities and the potential of our technology platform. Alongside our CF program, these proceeds will be used to accelerate development of ARCT-2601 for OTC deficiency, the first mRNA therapeutic to utilize our LUNAR 2.0 delivery platform.”
Joseph Payne, President And CEO Of Arcturus Therapeutics

articles.title: Alta Raises $47.5 Million for Its Compliance-Focused Blockchain
articles.snippet: Alta Raises $47.5 Million for Its Compliance-Focused Blockchain BlockTelegraph
articles.text:
What to know
Alta announced a $47.5 million Series A led by Index Ventures.
The company is developing a blockchain with compliance features for banks and large businesses.
Airwallex is both an early backer and a channel encouraging customers to use Alta for crypto transactions.
Alta has raised $47.5 million in a Series A round to build a compliance-focused blockchain for banks and large companies. Index Ventures led the round, which Alta announced Tuesday, according to Fortune’s report .
The company is developing its own blockchain with a compliance layer that lets customers ensure processed transactions follow rules and regulations around the world. Alta is pitching the system to financial firms and large companies seeking faster money transfers with crypto.
Why Alta Is Building a Compliance-Focused Blockchain
Financial firms already have a choice of networks, including Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche. Alta chief executive Loong Wang told Fortune he believes blockchain is the best technology for transferring money, but said existing options lack privacy and compliance tools designed for banks and other large financial players. Glass office tower viewed from below beneath clouds.
Wang said Alta’s features include a tool that prevents people from sending funds at random to addresses on its blockchain. The feature addresses a practice known as an airdrop, which can require wallet holders to accept funds whether they want them or not.
“We often say we wouldn’t have built an L-1 if we didn’t have to,” Wang told Fortune. His comments describe the company’s rationale for creating another network despite the many Layer 1 blockchains already available.
Airwallex Provides a Distribution Connection
Alta previously raised $32.5 million in seed funding, backed primarily by Airwallex, the Australian fintech company competing with Stripe and others in global payments. Alta has 25 employees and offices in San Francisco and Melbourne.
Fortune reported that Wang has a personal connection with Airwallex chief executive Jack Zhang. Zhang had been skeptical of crypto, but recently acknowledged the inherent value of stablecoins for cheap and efficient money transfers.
Airwallex is also serving as a distribution channel, encouraging its global customer network to use Alta’s platform for crypto transactions. The relationship comes as Airwallex rivals build crypto infrastructure too, including Stripe and its Tempo blockchain.
“With the rise of agentic banking and programmable payments, stablecoins are becoming an important vector for settlement,” Zhang said in a statement announcing Alta’s funding round.
Investors Join Alta’s Series A
GV (Google Ventures), Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg and Capital49 also participated in the Series A. Capital49 is a venture firm established by Airwallex’s cofounders. The company did not disclose its valuation in the round.
Alta was previously known as Metal and recently rebranded. Wang founded an earlier crypto startup that he sold in 2021, then pivoted to a second startup using quantum computing to aid drug discovery before returning to crypto technology to found Alta with Catherine Porter, a former Meta executive.
The round places Alta among companies building transaction infrastructure for institutional crypto use. Banks are also exploring stablecoin settlement and digital asset infrastructure, including efforts discussed at MERGE Madrid 2026 . Funding
Mosaic Raises $47M Seed to Develop Spatial Intelligence for Surgery
Published
November 10, 2026
By
Nova Jain, AI Entrepreneurship & Founders AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Mosaic Intelligence Labs announced on November 10, 2026 that it had emerged from stealth with $47 million in seed funding to develop sensing-enabled spatial intelligence and robotic systems for surgery, initially focusing on procedures performed through the vascular system.
The San Francisco company named 8VC, Fundomo, Lingotto Innovation and Obvious Ventures among its backers. Chief executive Ileana Pirozzi and chief technology officer Alison “Ali” Kight Mackanic founded Mosaic after meeting during their doctoral studies at Stanford. Their work alongside clinicians exposed how difficult, less-invasive procedures often remain tied to knowledge held by individual operators.
“We kept returning to one question: what would it take to scale the knowledge of the very best surgeons?” Pirozzi said. “We believe that starts with making our machines aware, and turning surgical repetition into experience we can learn from.”
Starting With Endovascular Procedures
Mosaic’s initial target is endovascular care. In these procedures, physicians thread flexible wires and catheters through blood vessels to reach treatment sites. Mosaic describes blood vessels as routes to virtually every organ, yet operators have no direct line of sight inside them. They use live X-ray imaging, preoperative scans and the feel of the instruments to work out where they are and what lies ahead.
The company identifies radiation exposure and outcomes that vary with operator experience as limitations of that workflow. Interpreting the available signals can take years of practice, and much of the resulting knowledge is difficult to record or hand down. The result is a mismatch: surgical access has become less invasive, while navigation still depends heavily on the perception and judgment of the person holding the instrument.
For context, Mosaic’s website compares open surgery’s 20–30 cm incision and keyhole surgery’s 1–2 cm ports with endovascular surgery’s 2 mm needle puncture, and lists stopping strokes, clearing blocked coronary arteries, repairing aneurysms and restoring blood flow to limbs among current applications. That range helps explain why Mosaic is treating vascular navigation as a reusable capability across multiple procedures.
Giving Surgical Instruments a Learning Loop
The technical design begins by instrumenting the point where surgical tools meet anatomy. Mosaic intends to combine those sensor readings with computation that reconstructs the vascular environment from within, maintaining a three-dimensional picture of anatomy and instrument position as it changes. A robotic interface would support precise instrument control.
The learning architecture would record the environment, instrument movement and physician actions as synchronized streams. Physical models would then help the system relate what it senses to what happens when it moves. The release connects this approach to the robotics concept of a world model: a representation of an environment that helps a machine predict how its actions will change that environment.

Business & Markets · Startups
Mount Thor Raises $45M in Funding to Expand AI Cloud Infrastructure on Apple Hardware
By Greg Bock · 12 November 2026 · 2 min read
Insider Brief
San Francisco startup Mount Thor raised $45 million in seed and Series A equity funding to expand cloud infrastructure providing on-demand access to Apple’s macOS operating system and silicon for AI development.
CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A, while Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the seed round, with additional non-dilutive financing secured for hardware purchases.
Mount Thor plans to expand computing capacity and develop infrastructure for AI agent training, software testing, long-running autonomous tasks and inference using open-source models optimized for Apple silicon.
San Francisco startup Mount Thor has raised $45 million in seed and Series A equity funding to expand cloud infrastructure that gives AI developers on-demand access to Apple’s macOS operating system and silicon.
According to the company , CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A, while Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the seed round. Other investors included CSC Leasing, Enea Capital, Long Journey Ventures and Upper90 , along with individuals associated with Cognition, Core Automation, Daytona, Meta, OpenAI, Together AI and Vercel. The company also secured an undisclosed amount of non-dilutive capital to purchase hardware.
Founded in 2026, Mount Thor develops and operates data center systems built around Apple hardware, providing computing resources for AI research, software development and running AI models.
The financing will support additional computing capacity and hiring, particularly as the company develops infrastructure for running open-source AI models on Apple silicon.
Building Infrastructure for AI Agents
Mount Thor is focused on developers of AI agents that use computers to perform tasks, including those requiring software available only on macOS, by building and managing rack-scale systems of Apple hardware to allow customers to access computing environments remotely rather than maintain their own equipment.
“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”
Mount Thor identified several uses for the infrastructure:
AI research: Creating reinforcement learning environments for computer-use models.
Agent testing: Providing secure macOS environments for developing and evaluating AI agents.
Long-running operations: Supporting agents that operate for weeks across a user’s devices using the same Apple identity.
Software development: Building, testing and simulating applications for Apple devices.
AI inference: Running open-source models optimized for Apple silicon.
Mount Thor reported deploying its first data center in less than six months and plans to increase capacity as demand grows. Its team includes people who previously developed infrastructure at Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI and xAI.

Some agents are designed to work independently for extended periods, while others respond to requests as they arrive. These capabilities create new infrastructure requirements, particularly when agents need access to desktop environments to perform their assigned work.
However, conventional cloud computing systems do not always provide the software compatibility these operations require. Applications designed specifically for macOS, along with features available through Apple’s ecosystem, can make Mac hardware necessary for certain development and deployment tasks.
Mount Thor provides remotely accessible Mac systems that let organisations create and run these environments without managing the physical equipment. The service targets research laboratories, software developers, and companies building AI-powered platforms.
Research teams could use the infrastructure to create different computing environments to evaluate AI models. This is especially relevant for systems trained to understand and control software through visual interfaces, where testing requires access to real desktop environments.
Businesses developing autonomous agent platforms could also use Mount Thor’s machines to provide individual macOS workspaces. These environments could remain active for weeks, allowing agents to keep working on tasks without a human physically operating a computer.
